facts.statement: Wear the shoulder belt across the chest and shoulder with very little slack.
Do not route the shoulder belt beneath the arm.
Do not route the shoulder belt behind the back.
Incorrect shoulder-belt placement can cause serious internal injury in a crash.
After fastening, tighten the lap belt low across the hips.
An automatic shoulder belt still requires fastening the separate lap belt.
Without the lap belt, a rider may slide out of an automatic shoulder belt in a collision.
Sit upright with the back against the seat and the feet on the floor.
Slouching or placing feet on the dashboard can reduce restraint effectiveness.
Wear a safety belt even in a vehicle equipped with airbags.
The handbook states that children below 14 must ride restrained in the rear seat while the vehicle moves.
Airbags are supplemental restraints intended to work with safety belts.
Airbags help reduce the chance of the head or upper body striking the vehicle interior.
Airbags distribute crash forces across the body to help reduce serious injury.
An airbag deploys only once and deflates rapidly, so it will not help during a secondary collision.
Safety belts position the body for airbag protection and restrain it in initial and later impacts.
Front airbags are designed for frontal or near-frontal impacts.
Front airbags are not designed to deploy for side impacts, rear impacts or rollovers.
Rapid airbag inflation creates force that can injure someone contacting the deploying bag.
Airbag-deployment injuries are usually minor burns or abrasions.
Being very close to a deploying airbag can cause serious or fatal injury.
In most vehicles, leave at least 10 inches between the chest center and the steering-wheel center.
Consult the vehicle owner's manual for the correct seat adjustment with airbags.
Raise the seat, use a cushion or lower the steering wheel as needed to aim the airbag toward the chest rather than the face.
Keep hands on the outside of the steering wheel rather than across its airbag-deployment area.
The handbook warns against seating a child in the right-front passenger position, especially beside an airbag.
Children aged 12 or younger should sit in the back to avoid airbag injury.
A front-passenger airbag switch, when provided, disables that airbag in its off position.
Where a vehicle with no rear seat or a small rear seat has the switch, the handbook describes disabling the front-passenger airbag to carry a child aged 12 or younger in the right-front seat.
Read the owner's manual for the airbag equipment specific to the vehicle.
A child seat may fail to protect a child when incorrectly installed or used.
Check that children aged 12 or younger are properly restrained in the rear seat.
Never place a rear-facing child seat ahead of an active passenger airbag.
Use both the vehicle manual and the restraint manufacturer's directions for child-restraint details.
The handbook says most vehicles with no rear seat or a small rear seat have a passenger-airbag on-off switch as standard equipment.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: An airbag deploys once and deflates quickly, so it does not provide the same protection during a secondary collision.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: An airbag deploys only once and deflates rapidly, so it will not help during a secondary collision.
changed_existing_facts.issue: Does not provide the same protection weakens the source's will not be helpful and can imply residual secondary protection.

changed_existing_facts.original_statement: The handbook describes the passenger-airbag off switch as intended for transporting a child aged 12 or younger in a vehicle without a suitable rear seat.
changed_existing_facts.corrected_statement: Where a vehicle with no rear seat or a small rear seat has the switch, the handbook describes disabling the front-passenger airbag to carry a child aged 12 or younger in the right-front seat.
changed_existing_facts.issue: Without a suitable rear seat broadens the physical no-seat/small-seat categories, and the right-front destination is omitted.

debts.text: The source groups side-impact, rear-impact and rollover collisions in a statement requiring side-impact airbags for protection. The scope of that grouped equipment claim is unclear. Preserve the source assertion as typed debt rather than infer which current equipment protects in each collision type.
